claims.text: Wear performance is governed by competition between dislocation-mediated plasticity and grain-boundary-mediated cracking.
Microstructural evolution and defect formation under wear conditions influence the competition between plasticity and cracking.
Changing nano-scratch load alters coating microstructural evolution and defect formation.
Changing scratch speed alters coating microstructural evolution and defect formation.
Increasing load improves wear performance within the proposed operating range.
Increasing scratch speed improves wear performance within the proposed operating range.
Enhanced dislocation activity causes improved wear performance.
Enhanced grain-boundary sliding causes improved wear performance.
As-deposited coatings have minimal microstructural evolution and defect formation relative to the intervention condition.
Beyond critical load and scratch-speed ranges, coating microstructure and defect formation become unstable.
Wear performance degrades beyond the critical load and scratch-speed ranges.

contradictions.description: Microstructural instability beyond the proposed boundary is presented as an expected limitation in the boundary field, but the same observation is also presented as a falsifier. An expected out-of-range failure cannot by itself falsify the hypothesis.

The mechanism identifies grain-boundary-mediated cracking as the competing process, whereas the predicted benefit is attributed to grain-boundary sliding. The hypothesis does not explain the relationship between sliding and cracking or specify which grain-boundary response should dominate.
